question: How is a caution level condition presented to the crew?

options.text: By a red warning light together with a continuous aural alert and a bell
By a message on the navigation display and a single chime
By an aural alert alone, with no accompanying light at all
By the master caution lights together with an illuminated system annunciator

explanation: The master light captures attention and the system annunciator tells the crew which area of the airplane to look at.

question: What is the purpose of the system annunciator panel?

options.text: It displays the engine parameters after a display electronic unit has failed
It groups the caution annunciations by system so the crew can locate the failure
It repeats the fire warnings from the overhead fire protection panel
It shows the position of the electrical buses and the generators

explanation: It narrows the search from the whole flight deck to one overhead panel area.

question: What is the effect of pressing a master caution light?

options.text: It extinguishes the master caution and the system annunciator, arming them for the next fault
It cancels the underlying failure indication permanently until maintenance has reset it
It recalls all of the annunciations that have already been cancelled once
It silences all of the aural warnings for the remainder of the flight

explanation: Resetting the system is what allows a second, later failure to be recognised as new.

question: What does the recall function do?

options.text: It redisplays all the annunciations that are currently valid
It cancels all the cautions that are currently outstanding
It tests every annunciator light on the overhead panel
It displays a history of the failures since departure

explanation: After cancelling, the crew has no display of what is still wrong, and the recall restores that picture.

question: Why is the recall used during the preflight preparation?

options.text: To confirm that no outstanding caution exists before departure
To clear the faults recorded on the previous flight sector
To test the brightness of all the annunciator lights
To arm the master caution system for the flight ahead

explanation: It is the single action that reveals anything the crew has not yet noticed on an airplane they did not fly in.

question: What distinguishes a warning from a caution?

options.text: A warning requires immediate action, a caution requires awareness and timely action
A warning appears only in flight, while a caution appears on the ground as well
A caution can be cancelled but a warning has to run until it is resolved
A warning is always aural, while a caution is always purely visual

explanation: The alerting level is a statement about how much time the crew has, which is why the colours and sounds differ.

question: Why are warnings presented in more than one sensory channel?

options.text: Because the aural warnings can fail independently of the visual indications
Because a crew member may be looking away or occupied when the condition occurs
Because a single channel would be inhibited during the takeoff roll
Because the regulations require two independent warnings for each case

explanation: Combining sound, light and sometimes touch means the alert does not depend on where the crew happens to be looking.

question: What does the takeoff configuration warning monitor?

options.text: The flaps, stabiliser trim, speedbrake and parking brake settings
The cabin pressurisation configuration and the outflow valve position
The landing gear position and the doors after the airplane lifts off
The engine parameters and the thrust setting during the takeoff roll

explanation: Each of these has been the cause of accidents, and the warning exists to catch them while the airplane is still stopping distance limited.

question: When does the takeoff configuration warning operate?

options.text: Whenever the airplane is on the ground with at least one engine running
On the ground, when takeoff thrust is advanced with an unsafe configuration
Continuously from the engine start until the airplane lifts off
Only once the thrust levers have reached the takeoff position

explanation: The warning is tied to the thrust advance because that is the moment the configuration becomes critical.

question: Why is a takeoff configuration warning during the takeoff roll treated as a reject?

options.text: Because the warning always indicates a problem with one of the engines
Because the warning almost always indicates a failed configuration sensor
Because the warning cannot be silenced once it has started sounding
Because the airplane may be in a configuration from which it cannot safely fly

explanation: The warning means the airplane is not ready to fly, and the runway remaining is the only remedy available.

question: What does the landing gear configuration warning compare?

options.text: The gear position with the autobrake selection and the speedbrake lever
The gear position with the flap setting and the thrust lever position
The gear position with the radio altitude and nothing else
The gear position with the airspeed and the flap placard speed

explanation: The combination identifies an airplane being configured for landing without the gear extended.

question: Why can the landing gear warning not be silenced in all conditions?

options.text: Because the warning horn is powered directly from the hot battery bus and cannot be isolated
Because the warning horn has no cutout switch fitted anywhere on the flight deck
Because the horn shares its circuit with the fire warning bell in the same panel
Because in the landing configuration the condition is genuinely unsafe and must not be ignored

explanation: Allowing a permanent silence would defeat the purpose of the last barrier against a gear up landing.

question: What aural warning indicates that the maximum operating speed has been exceeded?

options.text: An intermittent chime
A voice annunciation
A repetitive clacker
A continuous horn

explanation: A distinctive sound is used so the condition is recognised without reference to the display.

question: What is the purpose of the altitude alert system?

options.text: It warns the crew of proximity to the terrain below the airplane
It alerts the crew when the altimeter setting has been entered wrongly
It warns the crew of a cabin altitude exceedance in the climb
It alerts the crew when approaching or deviating from the selected altitude

explanation: Level busts are a common error, and the alert marks both the approach to the level and any subsequent departure from it.

question: Why is the altitude alert inhibited in the landing configuration?

options.text: Because the alert would then conflict with the terrain warnings at that stage
Because the alerting system is powered only with the landing gear up
Because a deliberate descent through the selected altitude is normal at that stage
Because the selected altitude is not used below the transition level

explanation: An alert that sounds on every approach would train the crew to ignore it.

question: What does the same intermittent horn indicate in flight that it indicates differently on the ground?

options.text: Landing gear position in flight and parking brake on the ground
Overspeed in flight and engine fire on the ground
Cabin altitude in flight and takeoff configuration on the ground
Autopilot disconnect in flight and door open on the ground

explanation: Using one sound for two conditions works because the two can never be confused in context, but the crew must know both meanings.

question: How is an approaching stall indicated to the crew?

options.text: By the autopilot disconnect warning
By a stick shaker on the control columns
By a horn and a red warning light
By an automatic nose down pitch input

explanation: A tactile warning is used because it is unmistakable and cannot be confused with any other alert.

question: From what is the stall warning derived?

options.text: Indicated airspeed alone
Pitch attitude and vertical speed
Angle of attack information
Flap position and gross weight

explanation: The wing stalls at an angle, not at a speed, which is why the warning is referenced to angle of attack in all conditions.

question: Why does the stall warning speed change with bank angle and weight?

options.text: Because the flap position limits the warning threshold that is used
Because the air data computer corrects the speed for the bank angle
Because the angle of attack for a given speed changes with the load factor
Because the warning system is calibrated for level flight only

explanation: A heavier or manoeuvring airplane reaches the critical angle at a higher speed, and the angle based system follows that automatically.

question: What is the primary purpose of the ground proximity warning system?

options.text: To warn of conflicting traffic below the airplane in time to react
To warn of an unsafe proximity to terrain in time for the crew to act
To provide terrain clearance guidance during the whole approach
To prevent a landing being made without the landing gear extended

explanation: It exists to break the chain in a controlled flight into terrain accident, where the airplane is under full control.

question: Which condition produces an excessive descent rate alert?

options.text: A high rate of descent above the fixed threshold at any altitude
A descent that goes below the selected altitude on the panel
A high rate of descent relative to the height above the terrain
A descent flown with the landing gear still retracted

explanation: The same rate is acceptable at altitude and dangerous near the ground, so the alert is always a function of both.

question: Which condition produces an excessive terrain closure rate alert?

options.text: The airplane is descending below the glideslope on an ILS approach
The radio altimeter has failed and gives no height information
The airplane is below the minimum safe altitude for that sector
The terrain is rising towards the airplane faster than it can be cleared

explanation: It protects against flying towards rising ground, which a descent rate alert alone would not detect.

question: Which condition produces an altitude loss after takeoff alert?

options.text: An early flap retraction after the takeoff
A failure to reach the acceleration altitude set
A climb rate below the required gradient
A loss of height after takeoff or during a go around

explanation: Height lost immediately after takeoff is close to unrecoverable, which is why it has its own dedicated mode.

question: Which condition produces an unsafe terrain clearance alert?

options.text: Flying above the maximum certificated altitude for that particular airplane
Approaching with an incorrect altimeter setting entered
Descending below the decision altitude during an approach
Flying too close to the terrain without being in the landing configuration

explanation: Being low is expected on approach with gear and flaps out, and unexpected in any other configuration.

question: Which condition produces a below glideslope alert?

options.text: Descending significantly below the glideslope on an ILS approach
Flying below the minimum descent altitude on a non precision approach
Intercepting the glideslope from above on an ILS approach
Descending below the selected altitude in the approach phase

explanation: Going low on the glideslope is a direct path towards the approach terrain, which is why it has a dedicated alert.

question: Which condition produces a bank angle alert?

options.text: A bank angle applied with the autopilot engaged
A bank angle exceeding the mode control panel limit
An excessive bank angle, particularly at low altitude
A bank angle held during an automatic approach

explanation: Bank near the ground reduces the available climb performance and brings a wingtip closer to the surface.

question: What is the difference between a terrain caution and a pull up warning?

options.text: The caution is purely visual, while the warning is both visual and aural
The caution gives time to assess, the warning requires an immediate escape manoeuvre
The caution can be inhibited by the crew, while the warning cannot be
The caution applies on the approach, while the warning applies only in the cruise

explanation: The two levels reflect the time remaining, and the warning means the manoeuvre must begin before analysing the situation.

question: What is the correct response to a pull up warning?

options.text: An immediate level off and a request for radar assistance
An immediate turn towards the lower terrain on one side
A reduction of the descent rate while assessing the situation
An immediate maximum thrust climb, following the escape procedure

explanation: The manoeuvre is flown first and the cause investigated afterwards, because the margin available is measured in seconds.

question: How does a terrain database improve on the basic system?

options.text: It allows terrain ahead of the airplane to be assessed rather than only what is below
It provides continuous terrain clearance guidance during the whole of an approach
It removes the need for a radio altimeter to be fitted at all
It replaces the need for the minimum safe altitude charts entirely

explanation: Looking only downwards gives very little warning of a cliff face, whereas a database allows the threat to be seen in advance.

question: How is terrain information displayed to the crew?

options.text: As coloured terrain on the navigation display
As a profile view on the primary flight display
As a numerical value on the control display unit
As an aural annunciation with no display at all

explanation: Showing the threat spatially lets the crew judge which direction offers an escape.

question: Why are inhibit switches provided for the ground proximity system?

options.text: To allow the whole system to be tested while the airplane is in flight
To disable the system altogether once it has been declared failed
To suppress alerts that would be nuisance alerts in known circumstances
To reduce the electrical load on the buses during the takeoff roll

explanation: A known operational situation can produce a valid but unhelpful alert, and the inhibit is a deliberate crew decision.

question: Why is the use of an inhibit switch a decision that requires care?

options.text: Because it disables the terrain display on both of the navigation displays
Because it cannot be reversed again at any point during the flight
Because it removes a protection that may be needed for a real condition
Because it also inhibits the traffic alerting system at the same time

explanation: Every inhibit trades a nuisance alert for a genuine loss of protection.

question: What does a windshear warning indicate?

options.text: A windshear condition has been encountered and requires immediate action
The airspeed trend vector shows the speed decreasing very rapidly
A forecast windshear condition exists at the destination airport
The crosswind component now exceeds the limit for the runway

explanation: The warning is generated by the airplane own sensing of what it is experiencing, not by a forecast.

question: Why is the windshear escape manoeuvre flown without changing the configuration?

options.text: Because the flaps cannot be retracted below the manoeuvring speed for the current setting
Because changing the configuration would reduce performance at the moment it is most needed
Because a change of configuration would disable the windshear warning itself
Because the landing gear doors would increase the drag during the escape

explanation: Every second of the encounter needs the maximum lift available, so the configuration is kept and the thrust is used.

question: Why are some warnings inhibited during a specific part of the takeoff?

options.text: To stop the alerts from triggering an automatic rejected takeoff at that stage of the roll
To keep the sensors from being read while they are unreliable at low speed
To reduce the electrical load on the systems during the takeoff roll
To avoid distracting the crew with alerts they cannot act on during the most critical seconds

explanation: Alerting a crew about something that cannot be acted on at that moment adds risk rather than removing it.

question: What is the significance of the priority given between different aural alerts?

options.text: All of the alerts sound at the same time so that the crew is given the full picture
Only one alert type is enabled in each phase of the flight so none overlap
The most time critical alert is heard first so the crew responds to the greatest threat
The alerts are heard in the order in which the conditions occurred

explanation: Simultaneous alerts would be unintelligible, and ordering them by urgency is what makes the response correct.

question: Why does a warning system test not prove that the sensed condition will be detected?

options.text: Because the test can only ever be performed while the airplane is on the ground
Because the test uses a simulated signal from that same sensing element
Because the test exercises the annunciation rather than the sensing element in service
Because the test does not include the aural output of the system

explanation: A test confirms the path from the system to the crew, and the crew still depends on the sensor doing its part.

question: What indicates that the autopilot has disengaged?

options.text: A flashing red light and an aural alert that must be cancelled
A single chime with no visual indication at all
An amber caution light with no accompanying aural alert
A message in the scratchpad of the control display unit

explanation: An unnoticed disengagement leaves nobody flying the airplane, which is why the alert is at warning level.

question: Why must a cancelled aural warning not be treated as a resolved condition?

options.text: Because the warning will repeat automatically after a fixed interval
Because cancelling the sound also cancels the visual indication
Because the system records every cancellation for maintenance
Because cancelling the sound does not remove the condition that produced it

explanation: Silence after a cancellation means only that the crew has acknowledged the alert.

question: Why are the warning systems largely independent of the systems they monitor?

options.text: So that they can be powered from the galley buses instead of from the main ones
So that the failure being monitored cannot also disable the warning of that failure
So that each of the warnings can be inhibited individually by the crew
So that they can be tested without affecting the normal operation

explanation: A warning that shares a power supply or a sensor with the system it watches can fail in the same event.

question: What is the value of a standard response to an alert?

options.text: It allows the alert to be cancelled far more quickly than it would otherwise be done
It produces a correct and immediate action without requiring analysis under time pressure
It removes the need to identify the underlying cause of the alert at all
It ensures the alert is recorded correctly for the maintenance system

explanation: Alerts occur at moments when there is no time for discussion, and the trained response is what closes that gap.

question: Why is the six pack annunciator arrangement useful during a failure?

options.text: It suppresses any further annunciations from the same system
It directs the crew to the correct overhead panel area immediately
It records the sequence in which the failures occurred
It displays the corrective action that is required

explanation: With a flight deck full of panels, knowing where to look is most of the diagnosis.
